newsitem.title: UK: Britain in new bid to ease N.Irish parades row.
newsitem.headline: Britain in new bid to ease N.Irish parades row.

text.p: Britain vowed on Sunday to step up efforts to find a peaceful solution to the row over parades between Northern Ireland's rival Protestants and Catholics.

Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, anxious to avert a repeat of turmoil that gripped the province last year, announced she would hold talks with pro-British Protestant marching groups and Irish Catholic objectors.

"The government is determined to do all all we can to avoid a repeat of last year's appalling events, which the people of Northern Ireland have made absolutely clear they don't want to see," she said in a speech in Manchester, northwest England.

Last year the province suffered its worst street violence for decades when police imposed a ban on a Protestant march in Portadown but reversed it after four days of riots and roadblocks by pro-British "Loyalists", triggering Catholic fury.
Trouble flared when police came under attack from both sides. Two Catholics were killed in more than a week of sectarian violence and many other civilians and police were hurt.

Mowlam's announcement came amid signs of continuing deadlock about a planned July 6 march from Drumcree in Portadown, ahead of the Orange Order's mammoth "Twelfth of July" parades which celebrate ancient victories over the native Irish.
The exclusively Protestant Orange Order aims to hold a march from a church in Drumcree, near Portadown, along a traditional route through Garvaghy Road which is a Catholic enclave.
Catholics, who consider Orange parades anti-Irish, have announced plans to hold a "street festival" at the same time. Protestants say the Catholics are aiming to block the road.
The Orange Order refuses to speak to most residents groups, claiming they have been inflitrated by hardline Irish republicans bent on wrecking Protestants' links with London.
The Order insists that its parades are not intended to be offensive but to display loyalty to the British Crown.
Mowlam said she would hold meetings with key groups which she met within days of her appointment after Labour ousted the Conservatives in a landslide election win on May 1.
"As of this week, I, along with senior officials, will undertake an intensive round of discussions with all the relevant parties. This will continue over the course of the next few weeks," she said.
"I want to give the opportunity to both sides in the debate to register their views on the best way forward."
The tension over parades is adding to community fears sparked by a renewal of hostilities by the Irish Republican Army and their Loyalist rivals.
Mowlam confirmed that the Portadown parade would be "high on the agenda", and promised to consider views on other problematic marches in the villages of Dunloy and Bellaghy.
